title: Mosaic colourwork fingerless mitts
subtitle: Two-colour slip-stitch mosaic fingerless mitts worked with one colour per round.
excerpt: Fingerless mitts in two-colour mosaic colourwork, worked by slipping stitches to create a geometric pattern. Only one colour is used per round so there is no stranding. DK weight, worked in the round. Afterthought thumb. Sized for hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm.
sourceNotes: Mosaic knitting (single-row slip-stitch colourwork) was documented by Barbara G. Walker in A Treasury of Knitting Patterns (1968) and in Mosaic Knitting (1976). The technique is well established; this fingerless mitt construction synthesises it with the standard DK mitt structure.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts x 28 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles. Mosaic fabric pulls tighter; swatch the specific chart.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Hand circumference 18 (20, 22) cm with 1 to 2 cm negative ease.

glossaryTerms.definition: A two-colour knitting technique where each round uses only one colour. Stitches in the non-working colour are slipped purlwise so they carry across from the previous round of that colour. The result looks like stranded colourwork but only one yarn is ever active.

A thumb opening made by working the thumb stitches in waste yarn during the hand, then returning after the hand is complete. The waste yarn is removed to reveal live stitches which are picked up and worked as the thumb.
A method for knitting small circumferences in the round on one long circular needle. The cable is pulled into a loop at the midpoint so each half of the stitches sits on its own needle tip.

Mosaic knitting uses only one yarn per round: the main colour knits its stitches and slips the contrast stitches purlwise with the yarn at the back; then the contrast colour knits its stitches on the following round and slips the main stitches. The slipped stitches span two rounds, creating a stepped geometric pattern without any floats. The construction uses
on a long circular. Budget about 60 g of MC (130 m / 142 yards) and 40 g of CC (88 m / 96 yards), both DK.

content.text: 22 stitches and 28 rounds to 10 cm in stocking stitch on 3.75 mm needles. Swatch the mosaic chart specifically as the slipped stitches pull the fabric narrower. If the swatch is 2 stitches per 10 cm too tight, try 4 mm needles for the mosaic section.

attrs.heading: Simple step mosaic (8-stitch repeat, 4-round repeat). MC rounds = odd; CC rounds = even. Slip all slipped stitches purlwise, yarn at back.

content.text: Before you cast on, circle your size. Every stitch count reads S (M, L) for hand circumferences 18 (20, 22) cm.
Using MC and the long-tail cast-on, cast on 40 (48, 48) stitches, a multiple of 8 in all sizes. Join to work in the round. Work 20 (22, 24) rounds of 2x2 rib in MC.
Join CC. Work the 4-round mosaic chart, repeating it for 5 (6, 6) full repeats. Total: 20 (24, 24) rounds of mosaic.
On a round 1 (MC) row: work the first 10 (12, 12) stitches with waste yarn in MC, slip back, and work in pattern to end. The thumb row lands on an all-MC round so the mosaic chart is not interrupted.
Continue the mosaic chart for 3 more full repeats (12 rounds). Bind off in MC.
Remove waste yarn and pick up 10 (12, 12) stitches above and 10 (12, 12) below. Work 14 (16, 16) rounds in 1x1 rib using MC. Bind off in rib.

Slipped stitches pulling in the fabric too tightly: the slipped stitches were drawn tight on each row. Slip each stitch very loosely, spreading the needle stitches wide before drawing the yarn across.
Colours appear on the wrong rounds: the MC and CC rounds were worked in the wrong order. Mark the first stitch of each round with a CC tail. The dark colour always works odd rounds.
Weave in all tails on the wrong side. The mosaic fabric benefits from a light wet-block to open the pattern.
Hand wash in cool water with wool-safe detergent. Lay flat to dry.
The same mosaic chart scales to a hat brim or a cowl at the same gauge. Extending the chart by 8 rounds vertically gives a deeper pattern repeat without changing the structure.
